page: Microsoft Azure NC96ads_A100_v4 is a high-density GPU-accelerated virtual machine designed for distributed deep learning, artificial intelligence inference, and parallel data analysis. The instance is powered by an x86_64 AMD EPYC 7V13 processor clocked at up to 3.7 GHz, delivering 96 dedicated physical cores with a one-to-one vCPU-to-thread allocation. The host architecture provides 880 GB of system RAM, yielding approximately 9.17 GB of memory per core. Hardware acceleration is provided by four NVIDIA Ampere A100 GPUs with a combined total of 320 GB of VRAM. Local high-speed caching and temporary data staging are supported by an integrated 4,115 GB NVMe SSD.

Benchmark results demonstrate top-tier execution across multi-threaded computational and AI workloads. In stress-ng multi-core testing and PassMark CPU suites, the machine ranks in the top ten percent of evaluated instances, showing high throughput in extended instructions and cryptography. Inference benchmarks highlight strong performance across large language models, delivering 3,485.82 tokens per second on 7B models and 499.27 tokens per second on 70B models during prompt processing. In-memory throughput is also top-tier, evidenced by 143.73 million Redis SET operations per second and cached read bandwidth exceeding 10,500 GB/s. In contrast, single-threaded metrics such as gzip compression and Geekbench text processing perform within the middle fifty percent, underscoring an architectural focus on horizontal parallelization rather than single-core frequency.

From a cost-efficiency perspective, the NC96ads_A100_v4 consolidates substantial GPU memory bandwidth, dedicated x86 cores, and local NVMe storage into a single host, minimizing multi-node network bottlenecks. However, running an instance with four enterprise GPUs represents significant resource density that would be inefficient for workloads lacking GPU integration or large-scale parallelism. This server type is best matched for training and fine-tuning medium-to-large generative AI models, multi-GPU LLM inference pipelines, ray tracing rendering tasks, and high-throughput scientific simulations requiring rapid scratch disk access.
